related_questions.question: How do I know if it's heartburn?

text_blocks.snippet: Heartburn is typically recognized by a burning sensation in the chest, often rising to the throat, and can be accompanied by a sour or bitter taste in the mouth. It's usually triggered or worsened by eating, lying down, or bending over. Other potential symptoms include burping, nausea, and a hoarse voice.

list.title: Burning sensation:
list.snippet: The most common symptom is a burning feeling behind the breastbone, which can radiate to the neck or throat.

list.title: Sour or bitter taste:
list.snippet: Stomach acid can cause a reflux of stomach contents, leading to a sour or bitter taste in the mouth.

list.title: Worsening with specific actions:
list.snippet: Heartburn is often more noticeable after eating, when lying down, or when bending over.

list.title: Other symptoms:
list.snippet: While not always present, other potential symptoms include burping, chest pain, nausea, a hoarse voice, or a prolonged cough.

list.title: Heartburn vs. Heart Attack:
list.snippet: While heartburn can mimic heart attack symptoms, it's crucial to seek immediate medical attention if you experience severe chest pain, especially if accompanied by pain in the neck, jaw, or back, nausea, and vomiting, as these could indicate a heart attack.

list.title: Heartburn vs. GERD:
list.snippet: Heartburn is a symptom of acid reflux, which can be occasional or infrequent. When heartburn becomes frequent and affects daily life, it is often categorized as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), according to NIH MedlinePlus Magazine.

related_questions.question: How to make heartburn go away?

text_blocks.snippet: Heartburn can often be relieved with lifestyle adjustments and over-the-counter medications. Maintaining a healthy weight, eating smaller meals, avoiding trigger foods (like spicy or acidic foods), and staying upright after eating can help prevent heartburn. Over-the-counter antacids or H2 blockers can also provide quick relief by neutralizing or reducing stomach acid.

list.title: Maintain a healthy weight:
list.snippet: Excess weight can put pressure on the stomach, increasing the likelihood of heartburn according to Scripps Health.

list.title: Eat smaller, more frequent meals:
list.snippet: This can prevent overfilling the stomach, which can trigger heartburn says Northwestern Medicine.

list.title: Identify and avoid trigger foods:
list.snippet: Common heartburn triggers include spicy foods, citrus fruits, chocolate, and caffeine.

list.title: Don't lie down immediately after eating:
list.snippet: Staying upright for a few hours after meals helps prevent stomach acid from flowing back into the esophagus according to HowStuffWorks.

list.title: Elevate the head of your bed:
list.snippet: This can help reduce nighttime heartburn by preventing stomach acid from traveling upwards.

list.title: Quit smoking and limit alcohol:
list.snippet: Both can irritate the stomach and worsen heartburn according to Scripps Health.

list.title: Manage stress:
list.snippet: Stress can slow digestion and contribute to heartburn.

list.title: Antacids:
list.snippet: These medications, such as Tums or Mylanta, neutralize stomach acid and provide quick but temporary relief.

list.title: H2 blockers:
list.snippet: These medications, like famotidine (Pepcid), reduce the amount of acid produced in the stomach and provide longer-lasting relief than antacids says Healthline.
Chewing gum: Chewing gum can stimulate saliva production, which can help neutralize stomach acid.

Herbal teas: Chamomile, licorice, and ginger tea may help relieve heartburn symptoms.
Yogurt: Some people find that yogurt can help coat and soothe the esophagus.
Avoid tight clothing: Tight clothing, especially around the waist, can put pressure on the stomach and exacerbate heartburn.

related_questions.question: What is the main cause of heartburn?

text_blocks.snippet: Heartburn, a burning sensation in the chest, is primarily caused by stomach acid flowing back into the esophagus. This happens when the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), a muscle that acts as a valve between the esophagus and stomach, doesn't close properly. Several factors can contribute to this, including certain foods, medications, and lifestyle choices.
snippet_highlighted_words: stomach acid flowing back into the esophagus

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at the causes:

list.snippet: The LES is supposed to prevent stomach acid from flowing back into the esophagus.
Weakness or improper relaxation of the LES can allow stomach acid to reflux.
Factors like pregnancy, hiatal hernia, or certain medications can affect the LES.
Foods: Certain foods can trigger or worsen heartburn by relaxing the LES or irritating the esophagus. Common culprits include:
Fatty and fried foods: They take longer to digest and can increase pressure in the stomach, potentially pushing acid back up.
Spicy foods: Can irritate the esophagus and increase acid production.
Citrus fruits and juices: Their acidity can irritate the esophagus.
Chocolate, peppermint, caffeine, and alcohol: These can relax the LES or stimulate acid production.
Tomatoes and tomato-based products: Can be acidic and irritating.
Large meals: Eating large meals can overfill the stomach, increasing the likelihood of acid reflux.
Eating close to bedtime: Lying down with a full stomach can exacerbate heartburn.
Obesity: Excess weight can put pressure on the abdomen, increasing the risk of acid reflux.
Smoking: Nicotine can relax the LES and increase stomach acid production.
Stress and anxiety: These can worsen heartburn symptoms.
Certain medications: Some medications, like aspirin, ibuprofen, and certain blood pressure or asthma medications, can irritate the esophagus or affect the LES.
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD): A chronic condition where stomach acid frequently flows back into the esophagus, causing heartburn and other symptoms.
Hiatal hernia: When part of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm into the chest cavity, weakening the LES.
Esophagitis: Inflammation of the esophagus, often caused by repeated acid reflux.
Delayed stomach emptying: Can lead to increased pressure in the stomach and reflux.
Musculoskeletal disorders: Certain conditions affecting the chest or back can contribute to heartburn.
Age: As people age, the LES may weaken, increasing the risk of heartburn.
